# Uppalavaṇṇātherīgāthā (Thig 11.1)

**ID:** Thig 11.1
**Section:** Therīgāthā (thig)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Uppalavaṇṇātherīgāthā
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/thig11.1
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0509m.mul10.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uppalavaṇṇātherīgāthā* (Thig 11.1) constitutes the eleventh chapter (*Ekādasakanipāta*) of the *Therīgāthā*, consisting of verses attributed to the eminent nun Uppalavaṇṇā [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In the text, Uppalavaṇṇā is confronted by Māra while meditating alone at the root of a *sāla* tree in the Blind Man's Grove [Sujato 2009]. Māra attempts to instill fear and lust, but Uppalavaṇṇā rebuffs him, declaring her complete detachment from sensual desire and professing her mastery of supernormal powers, including the feat of magically creating a four-horse chariot to pay homage at the Buddha's feet [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Collett 2014]. Scholars highlight a notable textual variation in this confrontation: whereas the parallel discourse in the *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* reads *dutiyā* ("companion/second") to praise her unmatched beauty, Therīgāthā 230 employs the masculine *dutiyo*, indicating that she possesses no male protector while secluded in the forest [Sujato 2009].

The biographical framing in Dhammapāla's commentary (*Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, Thī-a XI.1) embeds these stanzas within an extensive narrative of her renunciation involving incest, incorporating material from the *Apadāna* (*Thi-Ap* 19) [Silk 2009; Collett 2014]. This Theravāda exegetical account shares thematic connections with, yet differs significantly from, the elaborate tale of Utpalavarṇā found in the *Vinayavibhaṅga* of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* [Silk 2009; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Collett 2014]. In contrast to these narrative traditions, the canonical verses themselves focus strictly on her confrontation with Māra and her spiritual mastery [Collett 2014].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify the *Uppalavaṇṇāsutta* of the Pali *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (SN 5.5) as the direct verse counterpart [SuttaCentral]. Beyond Pali, the episode has parallels in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) [Bingenheimer; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus matches confirm deep Pali text reuse with the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* (43 matches), the *Uppalavaṇṇātherīapadāna* (Thi-Ap 19, especially segment §6.1–10.1), and the *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (§8.1–10.1 ↔ SN 5.5) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records shared verses with the *Khemātherīgāthā* (Thig 6.3, §11.1–12.4) and cross-language alignments with fascicle 12 of T 100, fascicles 39 and 45 of T 99, and minor phrase parallels in the *Lalitavistara* [DharmaNexus]. English translations of the text include versions by Ayya Soma and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
